chunks: Why coils are used in motors and solenoids. The question: Why are coils often used? What is so special about that configuration?
A single loop of wire makes only a tiny magnetic field.
Winding the wire into many turns makes each turn add its field to the others, so the total field grows with the number of turns.
That lets a small current from a modest supply produce a useful force. This is why motors and solenoids are built from coils, and why they behave like inductors.
Picture one person pushing a heavy cart. They barely move it. Two hundred people all pushing in the same direction move it easily.
Each turn of a coil is one pusher, and they all push the field the same way inside the coil.
The picture is only partly right: more turns also store more energy and slow down how quickly the current can change.
The field grows linearly with the number of turns at a fixed current. Two hundred turns of a 1 cm loop give about 12.
6 mT, 200 times a single turn; an iron core would multiply this by micro r until saturation.
Turn: one loop of wire. N is the number of turns. Ampere-turns ( NI ): turns times current. It sets how strong the magnetic push is.
Inductance ( L ): how strongly a coil resists changes in current. It grows as N squared ("What is inductance?")
Iron core: iron in the middle of a coil, which can make the field hundreds or thousands of times stronger. Winding: the coil of wire in a motor or solenoid.
A single loop of radius 1 cm carrying 1 amps makes about 63 µT at its center.
Wind 200 turns of the same loop and keep 1 amps, and the field is about 200 times 63 micro T equals 12. 6 mT. That is 200 times larger, with the same current.
The same ampere-turns can also come from fewer thicker turns at a higher current, or more thinner turns at a lower current, and, for the same amount of copper, the heating stays about the same.
That is the whole idea.

"A coil multiplies the magnetic effect of the current: each turn carries the same current and their fields add in the same direction inside the coil, so field and force scale with ampere-turns NI, and iron inside makes it far stronger.
The same configuration is an inductor with L proportional to N squared, so these loads store energy and resist current changes.
For fixed copper and ampere-turns, more turns means less current and more voltage with similar loss, so you pick turns to match the supply."
